doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Choosing Hamilton, Eddie Condon, and buying McNally's trombone
summary: His father took him to Condon's; he calls Emerson Brown about the Hamilton Dixieland band and buys McNally's 1932 Martin trombone.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: A good one. Although he didn’t last that long in high school music. In any event, so that’s about the time that I decided I wanted to go to Hamilton College. And I heard — great they had a Dixieland band. And I’d been listening. I was kind of brought up as a swing player but I’d been listening to Dixieland and my dad would occasionally take me down to New York to Eddie Condon’s. He was a great Condon fan and I became a great Condon fan. So I heard they had a Dixieland band at Hamilton and the leader was a guy named Emerson Brown. So I called Em up and told him who I was and I said, “Do you have a spot for a clarinetist?” He said, “No, because I’m the clarinetist and I’m the leader,” he said, “but we need a trombone player.” And I said, “I think I’ve got one for you.” So I went over to Chief McNally and he sold me his trombone, which was a great trombone, a 1932 Martin Committee model.

Well I have it but I don’t play it, it’s a little pea-shooter, but just a wonderful horn, I love it dearly. And he sold me that and I came to Hamilton not knowing how to play the trombone but knowing a lot about Dixieland music and basically that was how I got started.
That’s a great story, and you had great motivation to learn the music because you had, hopefully, a spot to go for it.
